description:
We are a passionate team of Peruvian developers driven by curiosity, creativity, and a desire to make a real impact through technology. We love solving complex problems, exploring bold ideas, and pushing our limits. We're looking for enthusiastic teammates with skills in software development, AI, data science, design, or scientific research. Above all, we value teamwork, innovation, and the willingness to learn.

From Peru to the universe! 🇵🇪🚀
summary: We developed ELIS, a platform that turns NASA FIRMS satellite data into one comparable fire record for Peru, 2000–2026. The satellites that measure fire changed: in 2012, VIIRS joined MODIS and began detecting many more small fires, so raw detections appear to jump 8.9-fold in one year. The fire did not change; the instrument did. ELIS corrects this with capture–recapture, the method ecologists use to count wildlife, comparing near-simultaneous passes of both satellites to estimate total fire, including fire neither saw. On held-out years, MODIS-only and VIIRS-only reconstructions differ by just 3.8% per year, and every estimate carries a 90% range. Two independent checks back the record: a machine-learning “synthetic MODIS” that predicts what MODIS would see from VIIRS data, and a Bayesian three-satellite model showing the sensors tend to miss the same fires, so our record is a conservative lower bound. This matters because agencies, regional governments and journalists in Peru need to compare fire seasons honestly, even after MODIS ends in 2027.
details:
The instrument changed, not the fire

Peru burns every dry season, and satellites are how we know how much. But the satellites changed. Since 2000, NASA’s MODIS has watched fire with 1 km pixels. In 2012 VIIRS joined, with 375 m pixels that catch many more small fires. Add their detections together and Peru goes from 10,375 detections in 2011 to 92,807 in 2012: a false 8.9-fold jump. It happens again in 2018 and 2023, as new VIIRS satellites launch. Anyone who compares fire years or builds a trend on those raw counts is measuring the satellites, not the fires.

What ELIS is

ELIS turns NASA FIRMS detections from five sensors (MODIS Terra and Aqua; VIIRS S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21) into one comparable fire record for Peru, 2000–2026. It covers the country, its three macroregions and its 25 departments. Our unit is the fire cell-day: a 0.1° cell, about 11 km, with fire on a given date. It tells you where and when fire was detected. It is not a count of fires or hectares, and we never present it as one.

Counting fire the way ecologists count wildlife

When two surveys see the same population, the overlap reveals how much both missed. We apply this idea, capture–recapture with the Chapman estimator, to two satellites. For each region and month, we compare the fire cells MODIS saw, the ones VIIRS saw, and the ones both saw, and estimate the total, including fire neither detected.

On the way we found something that changes the answer. Small fires flicker within an hour. When the satellites pass less than 20 minutes apart, they agree on 80% of MODIS’s fire cell-days. At 20–60 minutes apart, they agree on only 55–58%. So we calibrate only on near-simultaneous passes. With that calibration, the false 8.9-fold jump becomes 1.39-fold. Real variation survives: 2005 and 2010, known drought years, remain the highest of the MODIS era.

Tested on years it never saw

We held out 2021–2024 and never used those years to calibrate. On them, a record rebuilt only from MODIS and one rebuilt only from VIIRS differ by 3.8% per year for Peru (Amazon 2.3%, Andes 7.0%, Coast 9.0%). The naive sum of detections shows a 334% discrepancy on the same years. Against an independent reference from another satellite family, MapBiomas burned area from Landsat, the record correlates at 0.75.

Two more tools back the record:

  • A synthetic MODIS: a machine-learning model (AUC 0.76) that predicts what MODIS would see from VIIRS data, with a 3.2% annual error on 2013–2022.
  • A Bayesian three-satellite model, with a simulator: shows the satellites tend to miss the same fires.

What we do not claim

We state our limits on purpose. A record that hides them is not more solid, only less honest.

  • A lower bound: because the satellites miss the same fires, the record is likely about 10–15% low. No correction passed our tests, so none is applied.
  • A range on every estimate: each one carries a 90% range.
  • Labels kept separate: observations, estimates and forecasts are always labeled and never mixed.
  • Provisional recent data: data from August 2026 onward is near-real-time.

What you can do with it

At elis-peru.vercel.app, anyone can:

  • move through 26 years of fire on an interactive map;
  • switch between raw and harmonized data;
  • open NASA GIBS daily imagery with MODIS and VIIRS detections drawn at their real pixel size;
  • fly over the Andes in 3D;
  • read a seasonal outlook for 2027 by department;
  • simulate MODIS shutting down;
  • ask Ask Elis, an assistant whose answers are checked against our data.

Built to outlive MODIS

MODIS is expected to end its science mission in 2027, and the drifting Aqua orbit already sees 29% fewer fire cell-days than an on-time Aqua would. The ELIS record runs on VIIRS and stays the same without MODIS. Every day, an automated job publishes a sealed, hashed prediction of what MODIS will report and scores it the next day, so the link between the two instruments is checked in the open.

Why it matters

Fire agencies, regional governments and journalists in Peru need to know whether a season is unusual and where fire is growing. Today they risk answering from numbers that measure satellites. ELIS gives them a baseline they can trust, plus a seasonal outlook that beats climatology in backtests. Its 2026 August–October forecast contained the observed season within its 90% range. Trained on raw detections, the same model under-predicts every season after 2012 by a factor of 4.5. Without harmonization, even AI gets it wrong. FIRMS publishes the same data for every country, so the method can travel beyond Peru.

How we built it

Science and data: Python, DuckDB, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, NumPyro/JAX, Parquet

API: FastAPI, Uvicorn, Docker, pytest

Web: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS, hosted on Vercel

Automation: GitHub Actions for the daily sealed predictions

AI: Google Gemini for Ask Elis

Data:

  • NASA FIRMS
  • NASA GIBS / Worldview
  • NASA POWER
  • NOAA CPC ONI and ENFEN ICEN
  • MapBiomas Fuego Peru
  • INEI boundaries
  • Sentinel-2 cloudless (EOX), AWS Terrain Tiles and OpenFreeMap

The interface works in English and Spanish, and it keeps working from a static snapshot if the API is down. The team used AI coding assistants under its own direction; every method, data choice and result was defined and validated by the team.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS — Fire Information for Resource Management System (MODIS & VIIRS active fire data)
NASA FIRMS — Archive download (MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS 375 m, 2000–2026)
NASA FIRMS — Area API (near-real-time detections for daily sealed predictions)
VIIRS 375 m Active Fire product (VNP14IMG NRT)
NASA GIBS — Global Imagery Browse Services (satellite imagery layers in the app)
NASA POWER — precipitation and temperature (seasonal forecast predictors)
projectRefs: NOAA JPSS — VIIRS on NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 (active fire detections used via NASA FIRMS)
NOAA CPC — Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), seasonal forecast predictor
ENFEN / IGP — Coastal El Niño Index (ICEN), seasonal forecast predictor
MapBiomas Fuego Peru — Landsat burned area, independent validation (2001–2025)
INEI department boundaries (reference census limits, published by the SERFOR geoservice)
Sentinel-2 cloudless 2020 by EOX IT Services (Copernicus Sentinel data) — 3D basemap texture
AWS Terrain Tiles (Mapzen, Terrarium elevation) — 3D relief
Google Gemini API (gemini-3.1-flash-lite) — Ask Elis data assistant
DuckDB — analytical SQL engine for the data pipeline
FastAPI — public API and chat streaming
Remotion — programmatic video for the 30-second demo
Elis live feed — daily sealed predictions (our public repository)
